papers.title: Murmurations in Short Intervals for Elliptic Curves Ordered by Height
papers.label: arXiv:2611.33781v1

summary.background:
- Elliptic curve: a smooth curve given by a cubic equation, central to number theory.
- L-function: an analytic object encoding arithmetic information about a curve; its coefficients a_p are indexed by primes p.
- Root number (epsilon(E), a sign of plus or minus one): a weighting factor attached to each curve.
- Conductor: an integer measuring how "bad" a curve's reduction is; murmurations were first seen when grouping curves by conductor.
- Naive height: a different way of ranking curves by the size of their coefficients.
- Murmuration: an oscillating pattern in averages of epsilon(E)a_p(E) across curves, observed numerically and proven only in some settings.
- Averaging over an interval of primes: taking the mean over primes in a range (C1, C2).
summary.one_liner: The paper shows how short the range of primes (C1, C2) can be while still recovering the murmuration formula that Sawin and Sutherland proved for elliptic curves ordered by naive height, rather than averaging over all primes.
summary.plain: Mathematicians have noticed a wavy pattern in a statistic computed from elliptic curves, a common family of equations in number theory. This paper asks how narrow a band of prime numbers one can average over and still see the same wavy pattern in a previously proven result. The text indicates the authors determined how small that interval can be taken while keeping the conclusion of an earlier formula.
summary.why: It sharpens a known result by showing the averaging window can be made much smaller, which matters for understanding how the pattern arises. The excerpt does not say how far the window can shrink or what broader consequences follow, so its wider significance is unclear from this text alone.

papers.abstract: Murmurations are the phenomenon, first observed by He, Lee, Oliver, and Pozdnyakov (2025), that the average value of $\epsilon(E) a_p(E)$, the $p$-th $L$-function coefficient weighted by the root number, over elliptic curves of conductor in some range $N(E) \in [N_1, N_2]$ seem to approximate a continuous, oscillating function. While murmurations have been proven for other families of $L$-functions (notably by Zubrilina (2025) for weight $k$ modular forms), the only unconditional murmuration formula for elliptic curves is a partial result by Sawin and Sutherland (2025) ordering by naive height instead of conductor. In this setting, murmurations appear by first averaging $\epsilon(E) a_p(E)$ for a single curve over $p \in (C_1, C_2)$ and then average over elliptic curves of bounded height. However, Sawin and Sutherland's results average $\epsilon(E) a_n(E)$ over all of $\mathbb{N}$ instead of a small interval $(C_1, C_2).$ In this work, we prove how small the interval $(C_1, C_2)$ can be taken while preserving the conclusion of Sawin and Sutherland's first murmuration formula (Proposition 7).

papers.title: On the Distribution of Prime Factors of $\lfloor \alpha n^2 \rfloor$
papers.label: arXiv:2611.34913v1

summary.background:
- Prime number: a whole number greater than 1 divisible only by 1 and itself.
- omega(m): the number of distinct primes dividing m (e.g. omega(12) = 2, since 12 = 2^2 times 3).
- Typical size: omega(m) for a typical m up to N is about log log N, a result going back to Hardy and Ramanujan.
- Gaussian (normal) distribution: the familiar bell curve; convergence in distribution means the histogram of the rescaled values approaches this curve as N grows.
- Irrational vs rational: an irrational number cannot be written as a fraction of integers; a rational can. The two cases behave differently here.
- Floor function: floor(x) is the largest whole number not exceeding x.
summary.one_liner: The paper proves a central limit theorem for the number of distinct prime factors of floor(alpha n^2) over n up to N, for irrational alpha, and fully describes the distribution for rational alpha.
summary.plain: The paper asks how many different prime numbers divide a number of the form (a fixed positive number times n squared), rounded down, when n is picked at random from 1 to N. The authors show that after a standard rescaling, this count behaves like a bell-shaped (Gaussian) random variable as N grows, when the fixed number is irrational. They also work out the exact behaviour when the fixed number is a positive rational.
summary.why: This extends a classical line of results, in the style of the Erdos-Kac theorem for ordinary integers, to a sequence built from quadratic expressions with irrational scaling. The text does not say what applications it has, so its wider significance beyond this area is unclear to me.

papers.abstract: Let $\alpha > 0$ be irrational. We show that $\omega(\lfloor\alpha n^2\rfloor)$ obeys a Gaussian distribution. That is, for $n$ chosen uniformly at random from $\{1,\ldots,N\}$, the random variable $(\omega(\lfloor\alpha n^2\rfloor) - \log\log N)/\sqrt{\log\log N}$ converges in distribution to the standard Gaussian as $N$ tends to infinity. Additionally, we fully describe the distribution of $\omega(\lfloor\alpha n^2\rfloor)$ for a positive rational $\alpha$.

papers.title: An elliptic Lehmer bound of exponent one at a supersingular prime
papers.label: arXiv:2611.32749v1

summary.background:
- Elliptic curve: a smooth cubic curve with a group law on its points, studied over number fields (finite extensions of the rational numbers).
- Néron–Tate height: a canonical way of assigning a non-negative size to a point; it is zero exactly on torsion points (points of finite order).
- Degree D = [K(x(P)):K]: how many steps of field extension are needed to write down the x-coordinate of the point P; a measure of the point's arithmetic complexity.
- Lehmer-type bound: a lower bound saying nonzero heights cannot be arbitrarily small, here in terms of D.
- Good supersingular reduction at a prime: a condition on how the curve behaves when reduced modulo a prime, which is special and makes the curve's reduction unusually rigid.
- Elkies' result: a statement that every elliptic curve over Q has supersingular reduction at some prime, which is what lets the theorem apply to all curves over Q.
- Notation o(1): a quantity that tends to zero as D grows, so the bound is D to the power minus one, up to small corrections.
summary.one_liner: Proves a lower bound of the form D^{-1-o(1)} on the Néron–Tate height of non-torsion points on elliptic curves with good supersingular reduction at a prime, which by Elkies covers all elliptic curves over Q, improving earlier exponents due to Masser and to Hindry–Silverman.
summary.plain:
The paper studies how small a "height" (a measure of how complicated a point on a curve is) can be for points that are not of finite order. It shows that for elliptic curves with a certain good behaviour modulo a prime, such heights cannot drop below a bound that shrinks only slightly faster than one over the degree of the field generated by the point's coordinate. Via a result of Elkies, this applies to every elliptic curve over the rational numbers.</plain>
<parameter name="why">Lower bounds on heights of points are a central theme in Diophantine geometry, and this paper sharpens the known exponent from earlier work of Masser and of Hindry and Silverman. The text does not say what further consequences this has, so I cannot say more about its wider reach.

papers.abstract: Let $E$ be an elliptic curve over a number field $K$ with good supersingular reduction at a prime $\p$. We prove that the N\'eron--Tate height of every non-torsion $P\in E(\Kbar)$ satisfies $\hh_E(P)\ge c\,D^{-1}(\log3D)^{-1}\exp(-c'\sqrt{\log3D})$, where $D=[K(x(P)):K]$ and $c,c'>0$ depend only on $E$, $K$ and $\p$; so $\hh_E(P)\ge D^{-1-o(1)}$. By a result of Elkies this applies to every elliptic curve over $\QQ$, and it improves the exponents of Masser and of Hindry and Silverman.

papers.title: Counting elliptic curves by discriminant
papers.label: arXiv:2611.31390v1

summary.background:
- Elliptic curve: a smooth cubic curve with a rational point, the basic object of study in arithmetic geometry; over the rationals it is classified up to isomorphism by invariants c_4 and c_6.
- Discriminant: a whole number built from the curve's coefficients that measures how "degenerate" it is; the minimal discriminant uses the best integer model of the curve.
- Asymptotic formula: an expression saying how a count grows as a size bound X grows, here with an error term that is a power of X smaller than the main term ("power saving").
- abc conjecture: an unproven statement that bounds how often small integers can share large prime factors; it implies strong constraints on rational points and is assumed here.
- Cusp c_4^3 = c_6^2: the singular locus of the parameter space of curves, where the curves degenerate; counting integral points near it is the technical bottleneck.
- Q-isomorphism: two curves are counted as the same if they are related by a change of variables defined over the rationals.
summary.one_liner: The paper proves an asymptotic count with a power saving for rational elliptic curves ordered by minimal discriminant, conditionally on the abc conjecture, and gives an unconditional version for curves with an extra bound on c_4, using new bounds on integral points (c_4, c_6) near the cusp c_4^3 = c_6^2.
summary.plain: The paper asks how many elliptic curves over the rational numbers exist when they are sorted by a size measure called the minimal discriminant. It gives a precise formula for that count, with an error term that shrinks by a power of X, but the full result assumes the abc conjecture, an unproven statement about whole numbers. Without that assumption, the authors get the same formula only for a restricted subfamily of curves.
summary.why: Counting elliptic curves is a central question in arithmetic geometry, and an error term with a power saving is a much sharper statement than a bare asymptotic. The text does not say how these results compare with earlier work or what further applications they have, so the wider significance is unclear from this abstract alone.

papers.abstract: We prove an asymptotic formula with a power saving for the number of $\mathbb{Q}$-isomorphism classes of elliptic curves $E/\mathbb{Q}$ ordered by minimal discriminant, assuming the $abc$ conjecture. Unconditionally, we obtain the same asymptotic for the curves with $|\Delta_{\min}(E)| \le X$ and $c_4(E) \le X^{8/3 - \delta}$ for any fixed $\delta > 0$, by obtaining new bounds for the number of integral points $(c_4, c_6)$ near the cusp $c_4^3 = c_6^2$.

papers.title: The Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer formula for CM elliptic curves of analytic rank one
papers.label: arXiv:2611.29641v1

summary.background:
- Elliptic curve: the set of solutions to a cubic equation in two variables, with a natural group structure.
- Rational numbers: fractions; the paper considers solutions in rationals.
- Rank: how many independent rational solutions a curve has, in a loose sense.
- Complex multiplication: a special symmetry of a curve, tied to imaginary quadratic number fields.
- Analytic rank: a rank-like number read off from an analytic function (an infinite sum or product), which is conjectured to equal the algebraic rank.
- L-function: the analytic function attached to a curve whose behaviour at a specific point encodes the rank.
- Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture: the claim that the algebraic and analytic ranks agree and that a specific leading constant matches arithmetic data.
summary.one_liner: The paper proves the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer formula for elliptic curves over the rationals that have complex multiplication and analytic rank one.
summary.plain: The paper is about a family of equations of the form y² = cubic in x, called elliptic curves, which have a special symmetry called complex multiplication. These curves have a count of rational solutions, the "rank," and the paper concerns a conjectured formula linking that rank to a value computed from an analytic (infinite-sum) function attached to the curve. For the special case where that analytic count equals one, the author(s) prove the formula holds.
summary.why: The Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture is one of the Clay Millennium Prize problems, so a proof for a well-defined class of curves is a notable partial result. The text does not say how far the result extends beyond this class, so its wider significance is unclear from the abstract alone.

papers.abstract: In this article, we prove the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer formula for elliptic curves over the field of rational numbers with complex multiplication and analytic rank one.

papers.title: Elliptic curves with torsion Z/5: exact rank four over Q(k) and rank at least five infinitely often
papers.label: arXiv:2611.28977v1

summary.background:
- Elliptic curve: a smooth cubic curve with a group law on its rational points.
- Rational points: solutions whose coordinates are rational numbers; their group is finitely generated, with a finite torsion part and a free part of rank r.
- Rank: the number of independent points of infinite order; higher rank means more independent rational solutions.
- Torsion Z/5Z: the finite part of the group has five elements.
- Q(k): the curves depend on a parameter k, so this is a one-parameter family over the rationals.
- Elliptic surface and reduction modulo primes: a way to bound the rank from above by counting points over finite fields.
- Quadratic twist: a related curve obtained by a square-root-type modification, used here to add a condition.
- Genus-one curve: a curve of genus 1 with its own rank, here of rank two.
summary.one_liner: The paper constructs two elliptic curves over Q(k) with torsion Z/5Z and generic rank exactly 4 (with unconditional upper bounds via reduction of elliptic surfaces modulo primes), and uses a further quadratic-twist condition to obtain a fifth independent point, giving infinitely many rational elliptic curves with torsion Z/5Z and rank at least 5.
summary.plain: This paper is about elliptic curves, a family of smooth curves defined by cubic equations that carry a group structure, and specifically about how many independent "rational points" (solutions with rational coordinates) they can have. The authors write down two explicit families whose number of independent points is exactly four in general, and they check that no more exist using a modular-arithmetic argument. By adding one extra condition to one family, they find a fifth independent point and conclude there are infinitely many rational curves with at least five.
summary.why: Rank records for curves with a fixed small torsion group are a standard benchmark in arithmetic geometry, and this moves the known lower bound for that torsion from 4 to 5. The text does not discuss wider applications, so its connections beyond this area are unclear.

papers.abstract: We give two elliptic curves over $\mathbb{Q}(k)$ with torsion group $\mathbb{Z}/5\mathbb{Z}$ and rank exactly $4$, with four explicit independent points. The upper bounds come from reducing the relevant elliptic surfaces modulo suitable primes and are unconditional. They match the known lower bound for the generic rank with this torsion, due to Eroshkin, and are not isomorphic to Eroshkin's curve or to each other: their parametrising maps to $X_1(5)$ have degree $8$ instead of $12$, the constructions are dihedral rather than biquadratic, and their branch loci differ. In each case, two of the points come from a ``doubling'' step in the spirit of Jaswal. Adding one further condition to the second curve, coming from a quadratic twist over an intermediate conic, gives a fifth independent point over a genus-one curve of rank two. Hence there are infinitely many elliptic curves over $\mathbb{Q}$ with torsion $\mathbb{Z}/5\mathbb{Z}$ and rank at least $5$, improving the known bound $C(\mathbb{Z}/5\mathbb{Z})\ge 4$ to $C(\mathbb{Z}/5\mathbb{Z})\ge 5$.

papers.title: Splitting types of Richelot isogenies over finite fields and a newform of weight four
papers.label: arXiv:2611.27775v1

summary.background:
- A finite field F_q is a set with q elements, where q is a prime power; arithmetic is done modulo the field's structure.
- A square-free sextic is a degree-six polynomial with no repeated roots; splitting it into three monic quadratics is a factorization.
- A genus-2 curve is a curve of "genus" (number of holes) two; its Jacobian splits or relates to elliptic curves.
- A (2,2)-isogeny is a structure-preserving map between abelian varieties with a kernel of order four; the Richelot construction produces the dual quadratics.
- Splitting behaviour refers to whether a quadratic has roots in F_q or not.
- A newform is a special modular form; its trace of Frobenius is an integer tied to counting points mod p.
- The Legendre family is a standard family of elliptic curves; a twisted second moment is an averaged sum over that family.
- The paper says the value was evaluated for primes by Ahlgren and Ono.
summary.one_liner: Counts factorizations of square-free sextics over finite fields into three quadratics, with splitting conditions, via Richelot isogenies of genus-2 curves, with the answer expressed through the trace of a weight-4 newform of level 8 and a twisted second moment of the Legendre family.
summary.plain: This paper studies a counting problem: how many ways a polynomial of degree six, over a finite field with q elements, can be split into three quadratic pieces, when we also track which of those pieces factor further over the field. The authors give an exact formula for each of the 64 possible splitting patterns. The formulas involve a known number-theoretic quantity tied to a specific modular form, and the proof reduces the counting, by elementary means, to a known hypergeometric value.
summary.why: The result links a concrete counting question about polynomials and genus-2 curves to a specific modular form, which is a meaningful connection between two areas of number theory. The text does not say much about wider applications, so its broader significance is best judged by specialists.

papers.abstract: A factorization $f=uvw$ of a square-free sextic over a finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$ of odd characteristic into three monic quadratics defines a genus-2 curve with a rational $(2,2)$-isogeny kernel, and the Richelot construction attaches to it three dual quadratics $U,V,W$. We determine, for every odd prime power $q$, the number of such factorizations with prescribed splitting behaviour over $\mathbb{F}_q$ of all six quadratics. Each of the $64$ counts is $q(q-1)(q+1-n_f)/64$ times $C(q)\pm t_q$, where $n_f$ is the number of roots of $f$ in $\mathbb{F}_q$, $C$ is an explicit monic cubic, and $t_q$ is the trace of Frobenius attached to the newform $\eta(2z)^{4}\eta(4z)^{4}$ of weight $4$ and level $8$. The proof reduces the counts by elementary means to a twisted second moment of the Legendre family of elliptic curves, which is a value of a hypergeometric function over $\mathbb{F}_q$ evaluated by Ahlgren and Ono for primes. As consequences, the number of factorizations whose three pairwise resultants lie in one square class is a polynomial in $q$, with proportion $1/4+3/(4q^{2})+O(q^{-4})$. When the quotient is a product of two elliptic curves conjugate over $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$, we prove that the splitting of the factors $u,v,w$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$ decides which points of order two of the elliptic factor are divisible by two.

papers.title: An explicit Cassels--Tate pairing in characteristic $2$ and the parity of $2$-Selmer ranks
papers.label: arXiv:2611.27040v1

summary.background:
- Elliptic curve: a cubic curve with a group law on its rational points.
- Global field of characteristic 2: a function field or number field-like object where arithmetic is done modulo 2.
- Rank of A(K): the number of independent rational points of infinite order.
- Sha (Tate–Shafarevich group): obstructions to local solutions being global; its size is largely conjectural.
- 2-Selmer group and Cassels–Tate pairing: tools that detect elements of Sha and whose structure constrains ranks.
- Isogeny (Verschiebung) and 2-torsion: maps between curves and points of order 2.
- Artin–Schreier symbols: local pairing values used in characteristic 2.
- Local root numbers: local signs from the functional equation of L-functions, linked to parity of rank.
summary.one_liner: For ordinary elliptic curves over global fields of characteristic 2 with a rational 2-torsion point, the paper gives an explicit local-symbol formula for the Cassels–Tate pairing on the 2-torsion of Sha, relates it to Kramer's descent pairing and Milne's flat duality, and uses it to express the parity of rk A(K) + dim Sha(A/K)[2] via local terms and root numbers.
summary.plain: This paper studies elliptic curves, smooth curves defined by cubic equations, over number-like fields where arithmetic works in characteristic 2 (a setting where numbers behave like binary digits). It concerns a hidden group called Sha that measures how far certain rational solutions fail to exist globally despite existing locally. The authors give an explicit formula for a pairing that organises this hidden group and show it matches other known descriptions, which lets them determine the parity (even or odd) of a key count in terms of local data.
summary.why: Parity questions about ranks of rational points are central to arithmetic geometry, and the paper ties an algebraic pairing to local root numbers, a link that is of interest to specialists. The text does not indicate wider consequences beyond this setting, and the extension to prime order rational points, including the new case where the prime equals the characteristic, is presented as a technical advance.

papers.abstract: Let $K$ be a global field of characteristic $2$ and $\varphi\colon E\to E'$ the Verschiebung of an ordinary elliptic curve $E/K$ with a rational point of order $2$. We prove an explicit formula for the homogeneous-space Cassels--Tate pairing on $\Sha(E/K)[\varphi]$ as a sum of local Artin--Schreier symbols, show that it coincides with Kramer's descent pairing and, on $\Sha(E/K)[\varphi]$, with the pairing induced by Milne's flat duality, and deduce that it is non-degenerate on $\Sha(E/K)[\varphi]/\hat\varphi(\Sha(E'/K)[2])$. For every ordinary elliptic curve $A/K$ we express the parity of $\mathrm{rk}\,A(K)+\dim\Sha(A/K)[2]$ by local terms (after Kramer), and identify these with local root numbers at places of semistable or potentially multiplicative reduction, and in further cases using curves with finite $\Sha$. We determine $\Sha$ in examples, and extend the formula to rational points of any prime order $\ell$, the new case being $\ell=\operatorname{char}K$.

papers.title: Rational Elliptic Period Relations Across Realizations: Complex Lattices, Local p-adic Periods, and Drinfeld Modules
papers.label: arXiv:2611.25399v1

summary.background:
- Elliptic curve: a smooth cubic curve with a group law; its periods are integrals that encode its geometry.
- p-adic numbers (Q_p) and C_p: number systems built from a prime p, with a different notion of closeness than the real numbers; C_p is the completed algebraic closure of Q_p.
- Transcendence degree: the maximum number of algebraically independent quantities, i.e. how many values can be "free" with no polynomial relation among them.
- de Rham comparison periods: numbers relating two cohomology theories (algebraic de Rham and étale/Betti-type) for the same curve; they live in Fontaine's ring B_dR.
- Galois-stable line: a line of vectors fixed as a set by the symmetries of the field of definition.
- Ordinary and CM curves: "ordinary" is a condition on the reduction mod p; "CM" (complex multiplication) means the curve has extra symmetries.
- Katz's E_{2,p}: a p-adic modular form whose zeros are studied; the text uses its zeros as the special locus.
- Drinfeld modules: an analogue of elliptic curves over function fields.
summary.one_liner: The paper determines the algebraic relations among the full de Rham comparison periods of elliptic curves over finite extensions of Q_p, works out the transcendence degree and the Tate matrix, and analyzes ordinary non-CM curves at zeros of Katz's E_{2,p}.
summary.plain: The paper studies a family of numbers attached to elliptic curves (smooth cubic curves) when they are viewed through p-adic numbers, a different way of measuring size from the usual real one. It asks which polynomial equations these numbers must satisfy and which ones they can be free of. The text reports that the answers depend on the curve's structure, and it singles out special points, the zeros of a known function called Katz's E_{2,p}, where a rational quasi-period appears.
summary.why: The results give exact counts of independent quantities and sharp bounds on the degrees of relations, which is the kind of precise statement specialists look for in transcendence theory. The text also mentions an analogue for Drinfeld modules and a conditional arithmetic consequence for Katz values, but I have not checked how these connect to wider open problems, so the broader significance is unclear from the text alone.

papers.abstract: We determine the algebraic relations among full de Rham comparison periods of elliptic curves over finite extensions of $\mathbb Q_p$. The connected local monodromy group gives the transcendence degree and an explicit affine linear relation ideal for the full matrix in Fontaine's field $B_{\mathrm{dR}}$. After normalizing the holomorphic row and reducing to $\mathbb C_p$, the transcendence degree drops by one and the normalized determinant supplies the additional relation. Every polynomial relation of degree at most $d$ is detected modulo $t^{d+1}$. For $d\ge1$ this bound is sharp for each elliptic curve. A rational quasi-period row gives a Galois-stable Tate line. Together with an algebraic holomorphic period ratio it forces potential splitting, which identifies the exact ordinary CM obstruction. We compute the full Tate matrix. For ordinary non-CM curves with $p\ge5$, the standard quasi-period row is rational precisely at a zero of Katz's $E_{2,p}$. Away from the zeros the two full ratios are algebraically independent. At the zeros, a nonzero quasi-period and the normalized holomorphic ratio have algebraically independent images in $\mathbb C_p$. The complex question that motivates these results, the analogue for Drinfeld modules, and a conditional arithmetic consequence for Katz values complete the comparison.

papers.title: Equivariant iterated Eisenstein integrals for congruence subgroups of level 2
papers.label: arXiv:2611.26597v1

summary.background:
- Modular forms: functions on the upper half-plane that transform in a controlled way under a group of symmetries (here Γ(2) and Γ_0(2), subgroups of level 2).
- Eisenstein series: a standard family of modular forms; iterated Eisenstein integrals are repeated antiderivatives of them.
- Multiple zeta values: special real numbers defined by nested sums; cyclotomic versions involve roots of unity, and level 2 uses the simplest such case.
- Non-holomorphic: not complex-differentiable everywhere, involving complex conjugates.
- Single-valued polylogarithms: multi-valued functions adjusted so they have no ambiguity when going around loops.
- Lie algebra / Lie group: algebraic structures describing continuous symmetries; the paper works with generating series valued in such groups.
summary.one_liner: The paper constructs non-holomorphic "equivariant" iterated Eisenstein integrals for the level-2 congruence subgroups Γ(2) and Γ_0(2), built from level-2 cyclotomic multiple zeta values, and determines the Lie-bracket relations of the associated zeta generators.
summary.plain: The paper studies a family of special functions tied to symmetries of a geometric space (the upper half-plane, with rules for how its transformations act). Ordinary Eisenstein series behave well under these symmetries, but their antiderivatives do not, and the paper repairs this by adding correction terms built from certain special numbers and their complex conjugates. The construction is done for two specific symmetry groups of "level 2", and the result is checked by restricting to a particular weight, where it recovers known single-valued multiple polylogarithms.
summary.why: It extends Brown's known construction for the full modular group SL_2(Z) to smaller symmetry groups of level 2, which is a natural step in a long-running line of work on how modular forms and multiple zeta values fit together. The text does not claim wider applications, so its reach beyond this area is unclear from the abstract alone.

papers.abstract: The modular properties of holomorphic Eisenstein series for $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$ and its congruence subgroups do not carry over to their primitives. Instead, the transformation of iterated Eisenstein integrals under congruence subgroups of level $N$ introduces inhomogeneous terms comprising (among others) cyclotomic multiple zeta values of level $N$. We combine iterated Eisenstein integrals for the congruence subgroups of level $N=2$ of arbitrary iteration depth with their complex conjugates and (single-valued) level-2 cyclotomic multiple zeta values such that they define non-holomorphic modular forms. Our construction of these so-called equivariant iterated Eisenstein integrals for $Γ(2)$ and $Γ_0(2)$ proceeds at the level of generating series that take values in an infinite-dimensional (pro-unipotent) Lie group and closely follow Brown's analogous construction in the $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$ case. The required insertions of cyclotomic multiple zeta values are controlled by zeta generators for level 2 that normalise the corresponding (pro-nilpotent) Lie algebra of the generating series and whose Lie-bracket relations we determine systematically. Upon restriction to Eisenstein series of modular weight~2, we recover single-valued multiple polylogarithms on the genus 0 modular curve $Γ(2)\backslash \mathbb{H}$.

papers.title: On Hilbert's tenth problem for number fields
papers.label: arXiv:2611.24748v1

summary.background:
- Diophantine equation: a polynomial equation whose solutions are sought in whole numbers (or numbers from a given field).
- Hilbert's tenth problem: whether there is a general algorithm to decide if any Diophantine equation has a solution; the answer is negative over the integers.
- Diophantine definability: a set is Diophantine in a field if it is the set of solutions to some polynomial equation system with extra unknowns.
- Number field: a finite extension of the rational numbers, such as the field obtained by adjoining the square root of 2.
- abc conjecture: an unproven statement relating the prime factors of three numbers a, b, c with a + b = c; it is widely studied but not proven.
- Elliptic curve and rank: a curve defined by a cubic equation; its rank is the size of its free family of rational points, a measure of how many independent solutions it has.
summary.one_liner: Conditional on the abc conjecture holding over a number field K, the paper shows that the integers Z are Diophantine in K (hence Hilbert's tenth problem has a negative answer over K), and gives a more general criterion involving an elliptic curve of positive rank that does not gain rank over K.
summary.plain: This paper is about Hilbert's tenth problem, which asks for a general method to decide whether a polynomial equation with integer unknowns has a solution. The author works over number fields, which are extensions of the ordinary rational numbers. The paper shows that if a well-known open conjecture called the abc conjecture holds, then the ordinary whole numbers can be described by polynomial equations in these fields, which rules out a general solving method there.
summary.why: Hilbert's tenth problem was settled negatively over the integers by Matiyasevich and others, and the open question is whether the same holds over larger number fields. This result links that question to the abc conjecture, a major unproven statement about how prime factors add up, so it shows how one open problem could resolve another. The result is conditional on abc, so it does not settle the question outright.

papers.abstract: Given a quadratic number field $K$ we show that the $abc$ conjecture over $K$ implies that $\mathbb{Z}$ is Diophantine in $K$ and, hence, a negative answer to Hilbert's tenth problem over $K$. More generally, the same conclusions hold for an arbitrary number field $K$ provided that the $abc$ conjecture holds over $K$ and that there is an elliptic curve over $\mathbb{Q}$ whose rank is positive and does not increase over $K$.

papers.title: Superspecial curves of genus two over prime fields: Frobenius types and rational (2,2)-kernels
papers.label: arXiv:2611.23694v1

summary.background:
- Elliptic and genus-two curves: smooth algebraic curves; genus two means a curve with two "handles", and its Jacobian is a higher-dimensional group variety.
- Finite field F_p: arithmetic on integers modulo a prime p.
- Superspecial curve: a curve whose Jacobian is as highly symmetric as possible in characteristic p; these are the nodes of the graph.
- Frobenius endomorphism: the map raising coordinates to the p-th power; its action on Weierstrass points (the six branch points of a genus-two curve) determines a "Frobenius type".
- Weil polynomial: a polynomial encoding how many points a curve has over finite fields.
- (2,2)-isogeny / Richelot isogeny: a structured map between Jacobians whose kernel is a set of 2-torsion points; a "rational" kernel is one fixed by Frobenius.
- Class number and mass: counting invariants of imaginary quadratic fields; a mass is a weighted count of curves, with Eichler's mass formula used to compute it.
- Isogeny-based cryptography: schemes whose security relies on the difficulty of finding paths between such curves.
summary.one_liner: The paper classifies Frobenius types and rational (2,2)-kernels of superspecial genus-two curves over prime fields and proves class-number mass formulas for them, checked against enumeration for primes up to 173.
summary.plain: The paper studies a specific family of geometric curves over the integers modulo a prime, the kind used as building blocks in some proposed cryptosystems. It sorts these curves by how a basic symmetry (the Frobenius map) acts on their special points, and it counts the curves and the rational "kernels" (structures that link them to other curves) in each class. The counts are given by exact formulas involving class numbers, and they match a brute-force computation for all 37 primes from 7 to 173.
summary.why: The results give exact counts for the graph of connections that isogeny-based cryptography relies on, and the paper reports that this graph of rational Richelot isogenies is far from connected in the range computed, which bears on whether that graph can be used for cryptography. The text does not state any direct cryptographic consequence beyond this observation, so the practical impact is a matter for specialists to judge.

papers.abstract: Superspecial curves of genus two over a prime field $\mathbb{F}_p$, and the rational $(2,2)$-isogenies between their Jacobians, are the vertices and edges of the graph on which genus-two isogeny-based cryptography is built. Let $C$ be such a curve, with Jacobian $J$ and Frobenius endomorphism $π$. We show that $π^2 = p\,α_*$ for a unique automorphism $α$ of $C$ over $\mathbb{F}_p$ whose action on the Weierstrass points is the square of that of Frobenius. For $p \ge 7$ this gives the list of Frobenius types of the Weierstrass points: eight types, each with its Weil polynomial, a congruence condition on $p$, and its number 15, 3, 3, 7, 1, 1, 3 or 1 of $\mathbb{F}_p$-rational $(2,2)$-kernels; when all Weierstrass points are rational, the 2-Tate pairing on $J[2]$ is determined by $p \bmod 8$. We then prove closed formulas, in terms of class numbers of imaginary quadratic orders and of $ζ_{\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt p)}(-1)$, for the mass of the curves of each type and for the mass of the rational kernels whose quotient is a product of elliptic curves. For $π^2 = \pm p$ the total masses are due to Ibukiyama and to Xue and Yu; our proofs use the 2-adic Tate modules, the symmetry of the Richelot correspondence and Eichler's mass formula, and, for the other curves, modules over orders of a quartic CM field. The kernels are counted through gluings of supersingular elliptic curves. As a consequence, the proportion of rational kernels with decomposed quotient is of order $p^{-1/2}(1+L(1,χ))$, where $χ$ is the quadratic character of $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-p})$. All formulas agree with an exact enumeration for the 37 primes $7 \le p \le 173$. Finally we describe the graph of $\mathbb{F}_p$-rational Richelot isogenies, which is far from connected in the range computed, and discuss what these results say about its use in isogeny-based cryptography.

papers.title: $L^p$-norms of holomorphic cusp forms
papers.label: arXiv:2611.22226v1

summary.background:
- Modular surface: the quotient of the hyperbolic plane by the modular group, a standard curved space in number theory.
- Holomorphic cusp form of weight k: a complex-analytic function on that surface with special symmetry; "large weight" means k is big.
- L^p-norm: a generalized average size of a function; larger p emphasizes peaks. The sup norm (p = infinity) is the largest value.
- L^2-normalized: scaled so the total squared size equals one.
- Peak form: a form whose mass concentrates near one point.
- Poincaré series: a standard way to build a cusp form from a simple seed, indexed by an integer m.
- Asymptotic formula: an expression that matches the true size as the parameter grows, here with an explicit constant.
summary.one_liner: The paper determines the optimal orders of local and global L^p-norms of L^2-normalized holomorphic cusp forms of large weight on the modular surface for fixed 2<p≤∞, shows peak forms attain both orders, and gives an explicit-constant asymptotic for normalized Poincaré series over a range of index m.
summary.plain: This paper studies how "spread out" certain special smooth functions on a curved surface can be. These functions, called holomorphic cusp forms, are measured with a family of size yardsticks (L^p-norms). The authors find the best possible sizes of these measurements for large-weight forms, and show that functions concentrated at a single peak reach those extremes.
summary.why: Sizes of these functions govern how their energy is distributed over the surface, which matters for the study of quantum chaos and for bounds on the largest values (sup norms) such forms can take. The text gives only the abstract, so the wider connections are not established here.

papers.abstract: We determine the optimal orders of local and global $L^p$-norms of $L^2$-normalized holomorphic cusp forms of large weight on the modular surface, for fixed $2<p\leq\infty$. Both orders are attained by peak forms. For normalized Poincaré series of weight $k$ and index $m$, we obtain an asymptotic formula with an explicit constant, uniformly for $1\leq m\leq c_0k$ with any fixed $c_0<(4π)^{-1}$. We also give sup norm bounds in a wider range of indices.

papers.title: $\ell^p$-Improving for Discrete Fractional Integrals and Averages on the Moment Curve
papers.label: arXiv:2611.23137v1

summary.background:
- Discrete setting: functions live on integers rather than continuous space, so sums replace integrals.
- ℓ^p spaces: families of sequences whose p-th powers are summable; ℓ^p-improving means an operator maps a smaller ℓ^p space into a larger ℓ^q space.
- Fractional integral / average: a weighted sum (or mean) of values over nearby or structured points, with a smoothing effect.
- Moment curve: the curve (t, t^2, ..., t^d) in space, a standard object in additive combinatorics.
- Vinogradov system: a system of polynomial equations whose integer solutions are counted; "inhomogeneous" means the right-hand sides are shifted by constants.
- Diophantine counting: estimating how many integer solutions an equation system has, with N^ε meaning losses of size at most a power of N that is arbitrarily small.
summary.one_liner: The paper proves full-range ℓ^p-improving estimates for discrete fractional integral operators and (with N^ε losses) discrete averages along the moment curve, via essentially sharp Diophantine solution-counting bounds for inhomogeneous Vinogradov systems with an odd number of variables.
summary.plain: The paper studies how certain averaging and smoothing operations on whole numbers behave when they act on sets of points lying along a curved path, the "moment curve." It shows that these operations map small-exponent spaces into larger ones across essentially the full range of exponents, with one endpoint excluded and a small N^ε loss for the averages. The proofs rest on counting integer solutions to systems of equations, which the authors bound sharply.
summary.why: The text supports only a narrow claim: the results are sharp-type estimates within discrete harmonic analysis and analytic number theory. Its wider significance, such as links to other problems on curves or additive equations, is not stated in the text, so I cannot say more about it.

papers.abstract: We prove the $\ell^p$-improving estimates in the full range for discrete fractional integral operators on the moment curve (except at the endpoint) and discrete averages on the moment curve (with $N^ε$-losses). This follows via essentially sharp Diophantine solution counting estimates for inhomogeneous Vinogradov systems with an odd number of variables.

papers.title: On elliptic curves with prescribed analytic rank at least $2$
papers.label: arXiv:2611.21447v1

summary.background:
- Elliptic curve: a smooth cubic curve; its rational points form a group with a finite-rank part.
- Rank: the number of independent rational points of infinite order.
- Analytic rank: the order of vanishing at a central point of an L-function, a function encoding arithmetic data of the curve; it is conjecturally equal to the rank.
- Quadratic twist: a related curve obtained by a standard rescaling using a square-free integer.
- Congruent number curve: a curve whose rank determines whether a given integer is a congruent number (area of a right triangle with rational sides).
- GRH (Generalized Riemann Hypothesis): an unproven conjecture about the locations of zeros of L-functions; results assuming it are conditional.
- Zywina's result: unconditional proof that infinitely many elliptic curves over Q have rank 2.
summary.one_liner: Under the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, the paper shows every elliptic curve over Q has infinitely many quadratic twists with analytic rank 2 or 4, and infinitely many congruent number curves with odd analytic rank from 3 to 17, extending Zywina's recent result on rank 2 curves to the analytic setting.
summary.plain: The paper concerns elliptic curves, which are smooth curves defined by cubic equations and studied for their rational solutions. Each curve has a number, its rank, counting how many independent rational solutions it has, and an "analytic rank" that is a related quantity computed from a special function attached to the curve. The authors show, assuming a widely believed but unproven conjecture (GRH), that infinitely many curves in a standard family have analytic rank 2 or 4, and that infinitely many congruent number curves have odd analytic rank between 3 and 17.
summary.why: Whether elliptic curves of a given rank exist in infinite supply is a classical question in number theory, and the analytic version is easier to test with computable quantities. The result is conditional on GRH, so it is a partial step rather than a settled answer; its wider connections are to the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture, which links analytic rank to the rank itself.

papers.abstract: Zywina recently showed that infinitely many elliptic curves over $\mathbb{Q}$ have rank $2$, settling a long-standing open question. We explore the analytic version of this problem, showing that every elliptic curve over $\mathbb{Q}$ has infinitely many quadratic twists with analytic rank either $2$ or $4$, subject to GRH. We also obtain, under the same assumption, infinitely many congruent number curves with odd analytic rank between $3$ and $17$.

papers.title: On Erdős' last equation
papers.label: arXiv:2611.20783v1

summary.background:
- Diophantine equation: a polynomial equation whose solutions are required to be whole numbers.
- Positive integer: a whole number 1, 2, 3, and so on.
- Liminf (limit inferior): the smallest value a quantity approaches infinitely often as n grows; here it says the ratio is close to 0 for infinitely many n.
- Logarithm: a function that turns multiplicative growth into additive growth; log f(n)/log n compares the size of f(n) on a log scale.
- Erdős problems: a collection of open questions posed by the mathematician Paul Erdős.
summary.one_liner: The paper studies f(n), the number of solutions of the Diophantine equation n(x_1+...+x_n) = x_1...x_n, and shows that liminf of log f(n)/log n equals 0.
summary.plain: The paper looks at a equation about whole numbers: multiply n by the sum of n unknown whole numbers, and set that equal to their product. For each n, it counts how many solutions exist, and asks how that count grows as n gets large. The author shows that along some sequence of n, the count grows so slowly that its logarithm is negligible compared with log n.
summary.why: This is a question about the Erdős problem on the equation, and the result is a precise statement about how solution counts behave for large n. The text does not say how it connects to wider work, and the abstract alone does not show whether the methods are new.

papers.abstract: For a positive integer $n\ge 2$, we look at the number of solutions of the Diophantine equation $$ n(x_1+\cdots+x_n)=x_1\cdots x_n. $$ Denoting by $f(n)$ this number we show that $\liminf_{n\to\infty} \log f(n)/\log n=0$.
